page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.r9ae.large is a memory-optimized virtual machine operating on the KVM hypervisor platform. Built on the x86_64 instruction set, the instance is powered by an AMD EPYC 9T95 processor clocked at 2.25 GHz, providing 2 dedicated vCPUs. The hardware allocation delivers 16.0 GB of system memory, resulting in an 8.0 GB per-vCPU ratio that serves tasks requiring elevated memory headroom per execution thread without CPU contention.

Storage and network characteristics reflect a decoupled architecture. The ecs.r9ae.large comes with no bundled local storage, requiring attached network-based block storage for persistent file systems and boot operations. The configuration does not include discrete hardware accelerators or GPUs. Network performance is provisioned with a 2 Gbps baseline bandwidth, and complimentary public IPv4 addresses are not included.

With its 1:8 vCPU-to-memory balance, the instance provides qualitative cost efficiency for systems where standard 1:2 or 1:4 ratios force over-provisioning of CPU cores merely to satisfy memory requirements. Tradeoffs include low overall parallel compute throughput due to the two-core ceiling and network dependence for all storage I/O. Best-fit deployments include lightweight in-memory databases, Redis caches, staging environments, and memory-intensive background automation jobs.
description: Alibaba Cloud ecs.r9ae.large is an entry-tier memory-optimized instance built on the KVM hypervisor and x86_64 architecture. Driven by an AMD EPYC 9T95 processor running at 2.25 GHz, it supplies 2 dedicated vCPUs alongside 16.0 GB of memory, yielding 8.0 GB of RAM per core. The instance includes no local storage or hardware accelerators, relying entirely on network-attached storage solutions, and maintains a baseline networking bandwidth of 2 Gbps without default public IPv4 addressing. The configuration provides economic resource density for applications requiring moderate computing capability paired with substantial memory capacity. It is suitable for hosting small in-memory key-value caches, lightweight databases, microservice memory queues, and memory-bound background tasks.
